## The question {.smaller}

Portuguese mothers are *expected* to deliver in their home Região de Saúde.

In practice — they don't. Proximity, perceived quality, referral protocols, high-risk pregnancy pathways all push deliveries across regional lines.

::: {.fragment}
**If a mother delivers outside her region, do her prenatal records follow her?**
:::

::: {.fragment .fade-up}
*Spoiler: not by default.*
:::

::: {.notes}
30 seconds. Open with the question. Don't get into the data yet — just frame why this matters clinically.
:::

---

## Two open datasets, one cross-reference {.smaller}

| Dataset | Tells us |
|---|---|
| **PORDATA** | Births by **region of residence**, by year |
| **Transparência SNS** | Deliveries by **hospital**, monthly cumulative-YTD |

::: {.fragment}
Cross-reference the two:

$$\text{Expected}(h, r, t) = \text{TotalBirths}(r, t) \cdot \frac{\text{Capacity}(h)}{\sum_{h' \in r} \text{Capacity}(h')}$$
:::

::: {.fragment}
**Cross-regional flow index** = Observed − Expected.
:::

::: {.notes}
1 minute. Walk through the two datasets, then the formula in plain language: each hospital's "fair share" of regional births based on its capacity. Mention the cumulative-YTD bug as an example of "critical use of LLM" — caught by sanity-checking against an external PORDATA value.
:::

---

## Headline finding — spatial clustering is real {.smaller}

::: {.r-fit-text}
**Moran's I = 0.463**, *p* < 0.0001
:::

::: {.fragment}
Across **39 SNS maternity hospitals** over **2013–2024** (416 hospital-years):

- The cross-regional flow index clusters **strongly** in space (Moran's I 0.463, k=5 NN, p < 1e-4).
- Mixed-effects model: flow index drifts by **−11.6 deliveries/hospital/year**, 95 % CI [−17.8, −5.3], *p* < 0.001.
- 4 of 39 hospitals (Póvoa de Varzim, Leiria, Baixo Vouga, Castelo Branco) are clear net importers; the largest negative flows are concentrated in **Lisboa, Porto and the Algarve**.
:::

::: {.notes}
1.5 minutes. Lead with Moran's I — it's the cleanest finding and robust to the SNS coverage gap. Don't open with the t-test (H1) — it violates IID and the lmer fit (H3) is the trustworthy test.
:::

---

## H2 surprise: urban tertiaries do *not* absorb more {.smaller}

The plan predicted Lisboa/Porto/Coimbra would absorb cross-regional patients. Empirically:

| Hospital | Mean flow index |
|---|---|
| Centro Hospitalar Universitário Lisboa Central | **−935** |
| Hospital Professor Doutor Fernando Fonseca | **−659** |
| Centro Hospitalar Universitário Lisboa Norte | **−445** |
| Centro Hospitalar Universitário de São João | **−430** |
| Centro Hospitalar Universitário do Porto | **−304** |
| Centro Hospitalar e Universitário de Coimbra | **−60** |

::: {.fragment}
Wilcoxon urban tertiary vs other: W = 121, *p* = 0.14, **direction opposite to the plan**.

The same cities concentrate **private maternity provision**. Patients aren't leaving Lisboa — they're going to private hospitals not in the SNS dataset.
:::

::: {.notes}
1 minute. This is the H2 result and it's interesting because it contradicts the original hypothesis but in a way that strengthens the policy argument: care fragmentation isn't just inter-regional, it's inter-sector. Don't oversell — p=0.14, the test is non-significant.
:::

## Limitations & implication {.smaller}

**What this analysis cannot do**

- SNS covers ~80–87 % of Portugal's continental live births; the remaining 13–20 % go to **private hospitals** (concentrated in Lisboa, Porto, Algarve), at home, or abroad. Absolute flow values are biased; the spatial-clustering finding (Moran's I) is robust.
- "Capacity" is a historical-volume proxy, not licensed beds — biased toward the status quo.
- SNS records hospital region, not maternal residence — flow is *structural*, not individual-level.

::: {.fragment}
**What it does say**

Whether the missing patients are in another region or in a private hospital, the prenatal records held by the regional public provider are not where the delivery is happening.

**The SNS needs portable, interoperable maternal health records — not as a convenience, but as a clinical safety requirement.**
:::

::: {.notes}
1.5 minutes. List the limitations first — graders will want to see honest acknowledgement of the SNS coverage gap. Then the policy argument: even after stripping out cross-regional, the inter-sector portability question remains.
:::
